title: Send feedback from the Vercel CLI
description: The Vercel CLI now includes vercel feedback , which sends bugs, friction reports, and feature requests to the Vercel team from your terminal. Coding agents can also send feedback when they run into issues. Use vercel feedback with -f or --field to include structured context as key=value pairs. Repeat the flag to describe the task, expected behavior, and what went wrong. Update to the latest Vercel CLI and read the vercel feedback documentation to get started. Read more

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available now in AI Gateway
description: Kimi K3.1 Pro from Moonshot AI is now available on AI Gateway , along with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , a faster version for interactive use. K3.1 Pro is the first model in Moonshot's K3.1 series. It builds on Kimi K3 with improvements in coding, 3D modeling, financial analysis, and agentic tasks, and keeps the 1M-token context window and image input. For coding, K3.1 Pro handles work ranging from small fixes in an existing codebase to building a full project, including long agent runs with many steps. It builds front-end pages and interactive scenes with stronger typography and animation than earlier Kimi models. In finance, it can carry a task from start to finish, such as building a linked financial model with adjustable assumptions and scenarios, or writing research grounded in source documents. K3.1 Pro makes fewer factual errors than earlier Kimi models on difficult prompts. Moonshot AI plans to release the model weights by November 4: support for more providers will follow. Call either model through the AI SDK , the Chat Completions , Responses , and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. For Highspeed, use moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed in place of the model name below. Use moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro as the model name: To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro or moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try Kimi K3.1 Pro in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , Zero Data Retention support , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all language models available on AI Gateway. Read more

title: Baseten's Mammoth-1 and Elephant-1 now available on AI Gateway for free
description: Mammoth-1 and Elephant-1 from Baseten are now available for free on AI Gateway for one week. Free access is available through October 27. These decision models classify text, route requests, and score content against criteria you define. Mammoth-1 is the larger, 27B model, while Elephant-1 is a smaller, 9B option. Mammoth-1 is #1 on the Jev Decision Index and Elephant-1 is tied for #1 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. Both support a 16k-token context window and return choices, probabilities, and scores. Ask several questions about the same input in one request: select a support team with a Choice question, check for a refund request with a Boolean question, or rate urgency with a Score question. Your application chooses the probability threshold for acting automatically or sending a result for review. Use baseten/mammoth-1 or baseten/elephant-1 as the model name: See the decision models documentation for question types and additional usage details. AI Gateway provides a unified API for accessing models and tracking usage and cost. Decision calls appear in logs and count toward budgets alongside other model requests. Browse all decision models available on AI Gateway. Read more

title: Skipped monorepo deployments no longer count against limits
description: Deployments that Vercel automatically skips in a monorepo no longer count against your deployment rate limits. Teams with monorepos now get more deployments from the same limits. Vercel skips a project's deployment when its source code and internal dependencies haven't changed, using Turborepo 's package graph and lockfile analysis to determine which projects a commit affects. Skipping is enabled by default for new monorepo projects. You can turn it on for existing projects under Build and Deployment in the project's settings . Learn more about skipping unaffected projects and deployment limits . Read more

title: Making every harness durable
description: Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike. Running harnesses in the cloud Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products. These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt. In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work. Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox. Making every harness durable We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness , which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi , OpenCode , Codex , and Claude Code . It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts. With durable-harness , you can: Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance Make your local harness workflow durable Build your own durable harness Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back. What happens if its function times out while CI is still running? Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated. Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily. With durable-harness , a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log. Logs and queues durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World , the Workflow SDK’s durable backend. It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off. After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started: Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens. Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them. Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check. Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it. Pick your harness fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness. For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs . Runs everywhere Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching. Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World . durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code: On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World . In development, it uses files on your machine . On your own servers, it uses Postgres , MongoDB, Redis, or Turso. Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres. For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent: Check the self-hosting docs for more details. See every session in Agent Runs Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up. Tools An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again. Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools: A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically. A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice. The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund: For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on. Files When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations. To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options: virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox. virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn. sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox , with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work. Compare the three side by side in the docs . Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read , write , edit , and bash , and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace: For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace , and for fx, pass it to fxTools() . Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true . Each harness guide lists its built-in tools. Documents Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session. Tools can edit documents through io.docs , and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves: Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI: In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result. Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure . Wrapping up Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness , a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface. durable-harness is open source on GitHub . Read more
